messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Khun

Khun was forty-two when the shelling began in his neighborhood outside Phnom Penh. He had been a welder for the municipal water authority then, a steady man with steady hands, and he had stayed through the early fighting because leaving seemed more dangerous than remaining. The day that changed everything, he was walking home from the market when the first volley came—a sound like the sky cracking open, so loud it seemed to originate inside his own chest rather than from outside. He ran. The street fractured into chaos: people screaming, a child's shoe abandoned on the pavement, the smell of smoke and something else, something burnt that he would later understand was flesh. A building two blocks from where he stood collapsed in a cloud of dust. He made it home. His wife, Srey, was there. They locked the door as if locks mattered. That night, the shelling continued intermittently, and Khun sat by the window in the dark, listening to each distant concussion, trying to calculate whether the next one would be closer. He did not sleep.

Three days later, he and Srey left. They eventually reached a refugee camp in Thailand, then made their way to America in 1982 with papers and almost nothing else. Khun found work as a welder again—his hands remembered what his mind tried to forget—and for many years, he functioned. He and Srey had two children. He built a life. But the past did not dissolve; it only went quiet, waiting.

Now, at seventy-four, Khun lives in a small house on a tree-lined street in a modest neighborhood. He retired five years ago, though he still takes occasional welding jobs for a contractor he has known for decades. He and Srey have been married for fifty-two years. And yet, in the last year, something has shifted. He cannot quite articulate what, but the world has begun to feel dangerous again in ways that do not quite make sense to him.

The car sounds are the worst. A loud engine, a backfire, even the percussive rumble of a delivery truck—anything that carries that sudden, explosive quality—and Khun's body responds as though the shelling has resumed. His heart accelerates, his breath becomes shallow and tight, and for several seconds, he cannot seem to draw air into his lungs properly. The sensation terrifies him. He has come to believe that these episodes are warnings, that his body knows something his mind does not. He avoids driving now, and he has begun to avoid the main roads near his house. When Srey needs to go to the grocery store, he waits inside rather than accompany her, claiming fatigue. He no longer sits on the front porch in the evenings as he once did. The open space of the street, the exposure of being visible from the road, fills him with an unnamed dread.

His concentration has become unreliable. He will begin reading the newspaper and find that he has turned three pages without retaining a word. At night, he lies awake beside Srey, his mind alert and scanning, certain that something requires his vigilance. He does not know what. Sleep, when it comes, is shallow and interrupted. He wakes at small sounds—the house settling, a car passing—and it takes him long minutes to remember where he is.

When his daughter, Sophea, asked him recently about his reluctance to attend his grandson's school event in the gymnasium, Khun told her he was unwell. He could not explain that the thought of sitting in that large, open room—surrounded by people, with exits he would have to navigate—made him feel trapped in a way that contradicted itself. She did not press him, but he saw the worry in her face. He has said almost nothing to Srey about what he is experiencing. When she asks if something is wrong, he redirects, telling her about the news or asking about her day. The truth feels too large to speak aloud, and he is ashamed of it—this fear that has returned after forty years, this sense that he is not safe even now, even here, even at seventy-four.

What troubles him most is the quality of his own memories. He can see fragments—the dust, Srey's face in the doorway, the sound—but they feel discontinuous, as though someone else experienced them and he is simply watching from a distance. The whole thing seems impossible now, too extreme to have actually happened. And yet he carries a certainty that it was his fault somehow, that he made choices that day that brought the danger to his door, that he failed to protect what mattered. No one has ever been held accountable for what occurred. The injustice of that sits in his chest like a stone.

Last month, when a documentary about Southeast Asian conflicts came on television, Khun left the room without explanation. Srey found him in the garage an hour later, sitting in the dark. That night, he finally told her that he wanted to speak to someone. He did not know what help might look like, but he could no longer carry this alone. At his age, he had thought he was finished with the war. He is beginning to understand that the war, in some form, has never finished with him.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 74, but vignette describes Khun as 42 when the shelling began and now 74 — this is internally consistent, but the opening states he was 42 'when the shelling began,' implying the trauma occurred approximately 32 years ago (around 1992), whereas the vignette later indicates he left Cambodia in 1982 and the war would have been in the late 1970s/early 1980s. This creates a historical inconsistency rather than a demographics mismatch, but the framing is unclear.: The vignette accurately reflects: (1) Trauma type—civilian in war zone (Cambodian shelling, Phnom Penh); (2) Occupation—welder (explicitly mentioned multiple times); (3) Gender—male (conveyed through pronouns 'he/him'); (4) Age context—74 years old (explicitly stated). All four demographics fields are present. All reported symptoms are reflected: Triggers (car sounds causing breathlessness and panic), Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance of talking with Srey, redirection when asked about problems, avoidance of open spaces like the gymnasium and front porch), Threat symptoms (concentration difficulties, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance), Memory symptoms (fragmented/incomplete memories, feeling detached from the memory as though someone else experienced it, sense that the event is too extreme to be real), and Negative Appraisals (sense of injustice and lack of accountability, self-blame for choices that day). The vignette is comprehensive and clinically coherent.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

# Khun

Khun was forty-two years old in 1982 when he and his wife Srey finally left Cambodia, though the shelling that had fractured his world had come years earlier, in the late 1970s, during the fighting that consumed Phnom Penh. He had been a welder for the municipal water authority then, a steady man with steady hands, and he had stayed through the early fighting because leaving seemed more dangerous than remaining. The day that changed everything, he was walking home from the market when the first volley came—a sound like the sky cracking open, so loud it seemed to originate inside his own chest rather than from outside. He ran. The street fractured into chaos: people screaming, a child's shoe abandoned on the pavement, the smell of smoke and something else, something burnt that he would later understand was flesh. A building two blocks from where he stood collapsed in a cloud of dust. He made it home. His wife, Srey, was there. They locked the door as if locks mattered. That night, the shelling continued intermittently, and Khun sat by the window in the dark, listening to each distant concussion, trying to calculate whether the next one would be closer. He did not sleep. Within days, they fled, eventually reaching a refugee camp in Thailand before making their way to America with papers and almost nothing else.

Now, at seventy-four, Khun lives in a small house on a tree-lined street in a modest neighborhood. He retired five years ago, though he still takes occasional welding jobs for a contractor he has known for decades. He and Srey have been married for fifty-two years, and they have two adult children and grandchildren. For most of the decades since arriving in America, he functioned. He found work as a welder again—his hands remembered what his mind tried to forget—and he built a life that felt, on the surface, stable and whole. But the past did not dissolve; it only went quiet, waiting. In the last year, something has shifted. He cannot quite articulate what, but the world has begun to feel dangerous again in ways that do not quite make sense to him, and he is terrified by what this might mean.

The car sounds are the worst. A loud engine, a backfire, even the percussive rumble of a delivery truck—anything that carries that sudden, explosive quality—and Khun's body responds as though the shelling has resumed. His heart accelerates, his breath becomes shallow and tight, and for several seconds, he cannot seem to draw air into his lungs properly. The sensation terrifies him. He has come to believe that these episodes are warnings, that his body knows something his mind does not, that the world is as dangerous as it was then and he has somehow fooled himself into thinking otherwise. He avoids driving now, and he has begun to avoid the main roads near his house. When Srey needs to go to the grocery store, he waits inside rather than accompany her, claiming fatigue. He no longer sits on the front porch in the evenings as he once did. The open space of the street, the exposure of being visible from the road, fills him with an unnamed dread that he cannot justify but cannot shake. His concentration has become unreliable. He will begin reading the newspaper and find that he has turned three pages without retaining a word. At night, he lies awake beside Srey, his mind alert and scanning, certain that something requires his vigilance. He does not know what. Sleep, when it comes, is shallow and interrupted. He wakes at small sounds—the house settling, a car passing—and it takes him long minutes to remember where he is, who he is, that he is safe.

What troubles him most is the quality of his own memories. He can see fragments—the dust, Srey's face in the doorway, the sound—but they feel discontinuous, as though someone else experienced them and he is simply watching from a distance. The whole thing seems impossible now, too extreme to have actually happened, and yet he carries a certainty that it was his fault somehow, that he made choices that day that brought the danger to his door, that he failed to protect what mattered. No one has ever been held accountable for what occurred. The injustice of that sits in his chest like a stone. When his daughter, Sophea, asked him recently about his reluctance to attend his grandson's school event in the gymnasium, Khun told her he was unwell. He could not explain that the thought of sitting in that large, open room—surrounded by people, with exits he would have to navigate—made him feel trapped in a way that contradicted itself. She did not press him, but he saw the worry in her face. He has said almost nothing to Srey about what he is experiencing. When she asks if something is wrong, he redirects, telling her about the news or asking about her day. The truth feels too large to speak aloud, and he is ashamed of it—this fear that has returned after forty years, this sense that he is not safe even now, even here, even at seventy-four.

Last month, when a documentary about Southeast Asian conflicts came on television, Khun left the room without explanation. Srey found him in the garage an hour later, sitting in the dark. That night, he finally told her that he wanted to speak to someone. He did not know what help might look like, but he could no longer carry this alone. At his age, he had thought he was finished with the war. He is beginning to understand that the war, in some form, has never finished with him.
